# 2026-11-21: How information about the contact propagates through the body {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** promoted to @sec-parts · **Thread:** T2 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_propagation.py`
:::

**Question.** @sec-langevin found that, in a body thermalized by its own dampers, every
design holds the same information about the contact force, and designs differ in how much
of it a given part of the body holds. What decides how much reaches a part, and what
erodes it on the way?

**Findings.** A part of the body holds the contact force as if the contact damping
were larger than it is: it sees the force through an *effective contact damping*
$b_{\rm eff}(\omega)\ge b_c$. The ratio $\rho(\omega)=b_c/b_{\rm eff}(\omega)$, between 0 and
1, is the fraction that propagates to the part at frequency $\omega$. It falls below 1 for
one reason only: thermal noise from dampers inside the body that the force has to cross
on its way to the part. Inertia and compliance matter through how they shape that noise
at the part. With no internal damper, every part holds everything. On the SEA at
$k_s=70$ the joint-side link holds 98% of the body's information and the rotor, behind
the series damper, holds 6%.

**Where it lives now.** The definitions, proofs, figures and numbers moved to @sec-parts of
the chapter on information inside the body. This note keeps the dated record of the
question and what was found.
